name: Eastern & Oriental Hotel
label: E&O Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Farquhar' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lebuh Farquhar nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/816099544: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Eastern & Oriental Hotel' (353 m across).

text.description:
The Eastern & Oriental Hotel, usually called the E&O, is a British colonial-style hotel on the seafront in George Town. The Sarkies Brothers, who also founded Raffles in Singapore, opened the Eastern Hotel in 1884 and the Oriental Hotel the following year. The two merged in 1889, and the present complex was completed in 1929. After a long decline, the hotel closed in 1996 for major rebuilding. The front wing, now called the Heritage Wing, was restored, and the hotel reopened in 2001. A newer 132-room tower, the Victory Annex, was added in 2013.

It photographs well because the white Victorian façade is long, symmetrical and easy to read, and the sea sits behind it. The most recommended spot for the façade is Lebuh Farquhar, facing the Heritage Wing head-on. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the rooflines stay straight. The building is very wide, so leave some space around it rather than cropping tight. If you have time for a second picture, the approach outside the hotel entrance is a good place to photograph the grand front at sunset. Look out for passing traffic and people on the street, and wait for a gap before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: The hotel stands on the seafront in the heritage part of George Town, on the Lebuh Farquhar side, facing the sea.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for central George Town and walk to Lebuh Farquhar. From there, simply turn to face the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight, natural view of the façade. If you are close and the building will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as windows and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar (opposite the hotel's Heritage Wing facade, facing the building). The hotel's white Victorian façade head-on, framed by the street, with the sea behind it. The hotel is to the north of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so it does not lean. Centre the main entrance for a symmetrical shot, and leave a little street in the foreground. For a second view, try the hotel entrance and grand front at sunset from the approach outside the doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the white walls keep their detail and do not wash out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when light from the sea falls flat across the white façade. The entrance view works well at sunset.

text.access_note: Check on the ground whether the hotel's frontage and entrance area are open to the public.
claims_not_in_sources: Passing traffic and people may need to be waited out for a clear view of the façade.
Whether the hotel's frontage, lawn and entrance area are open to the public should be checked on the ground.

name: Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion
label: Blue Mansion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Leith' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lebuh Leith nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/247175848: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion' (79 m across).
notes: Indigo-blue courtyard mansion, a heritage icon.

text.description:
The Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion, often called the Blue Mansion, is one of the easiest buildings in George Town to pick out: a large house with deep indigo-blue walls on Leith Street. It was built at the end of the 19th century by the merchant Cheong Fatt Tze as his home and business base in Penang. It has 38 rooms, five granite-paved courtyards, seven staircases and 220 timber louvre windows. The blue comes from lime mixed with natural indigo dye, which also helped keep the house cool in the tropical climate. In 1989 a group of local people bought the mansion to save it from development, and it now runs as a hotel and museum. Its restoration won a UNESCO award in 2000, and it has appeared in films including Indochine and Crazy Rich Asians.

For a phone photo, the best free view is the whole street facade from across the road. The strong blue wall, the pale trim and the rows of windows give a clean, graphic picture, and the colour looks richest in soft light. Stand on the pavement opposite, keep the walls straight in the frame and watch for passing traffic. Stewart Lane gives a wider alternative with more sky and street. Inside, the courtyards and stained glass can only be seen on a guided tour, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The mansion stands on Leith Street (Lebuh Leith) in George Town, Penang. The viewpoint is on the opposite side of the street, facing its blue facade.
text.directions_text: Head for central George Town and make your way to Lebuh Leith. Once you are on the street, cross to the side opposite the mansion. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is tight and you want the whole facade in one frame. Otherwise the default lens (1x) gives a more natural, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as windows and trim.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lebuh Leith (opposite side of the street, facing the mansion's indigo facade). The full indigo-blue street facade of the mansion, framed straight on from across the road. For a wider view with more sky and street, try Stewart Lane instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the wall up with them so the building looks straight, not leaning. Keep the blue facade filling most of the frame, with a little pavement at the bottom. Wait for a gap in passing people or vehicles before you shoot. Stewart Lane is a good second option for a wider shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blue wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the indigo stays rich and does not wash out. Take a second shot with the telephoto for detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 10am or in the late afternoon, when the light is soft. One guide says strong afternoon sun washes out the colour.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the street, but the mansion is a working hotel and museum, and the interior is only open on guided tours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Pinang Peranakan Mansion
label: Peranakan Mansion
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12433499: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pinang Peranakan Mansion' (59 m across).
notes: Museum in a lavish Baba-Nyonya mansion.

text.description:
Pinang Peranakan Mansion is a museum on Church Street in George Town, dedicated to Penang's Peranakan heritage. The building was once the home and office of Chung Keng Quee, a wealthy 19th-century Chinese tycoon, and its green-painted front is easy to pick out among the neighbouring buildings. That colour gives your photos a clear focal point, especially against a bright sky.

Chung bought the land in 1893 and had the mansion built in the 1890s. It is described as Straits Eclectic in style, mixing European and Chinese ideas: there is a five foot way along the side of the building, and the inside has wide courtyards. The mansion was originally white. It was repainted green when a developer turned it into a museum in the 1990s. A temple honouring Chung stands next to it.

For your phone, the main picture is the outside of the building from the street. Stand back far enough to fit the whole front in, and keep your phone level so the straight lines of the facade don't lean. Then move in for details such as the doors, the carved woodwork and the colours. Inside there are thousands of Peranakan antiques and a grand long dining table, but whether you can photograph indoors is something to check with the museum. Church Street can have passing traffic and people, so wait for a gap before you take your shot.
text.geographic_location: The mansion is on Church Street in the heart of George Town, Penang. A temple honouring its original owner stands right next to it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are near this spot, so start from the centre of George Town and head for Church Street. The mansion is easy to recognise by its green front. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped at Pinang Peranakan Mansion on Church Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the mansion. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to step back, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the doors and carved woodwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It sits right at the middle of the mansion's outline, so you are on the spot itself and the building is all around you. For the classic view of the front, step back across Church Street where it is safe to do so, and look back at the green facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the edges of the building up with the vertical lines, so the walls stay straight. Put the green front in the middle with a little street in the foreground. Then take a second, closer shot of a doorway or a patterned detail. The temple next door makes a good second subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the green wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. Ultra-wide shots can stretch the edges of the frame, so keep people and signs away from the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the green paint shows its colour. Early morning is usually quieter on the street.

text.access_note: The mansion is a museum, so entry and photography rules inside may apply: check the official site before you go.

name: Clan Jetties
label: Chew Jetty
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chew Jetty' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chew Jetty' (relation/13314976): middle (253 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17443092: large area 'Clan Jetties' (756 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Stilt-house Chinese clan villages over the sea.

text.description:
The Clan Jetties are a row of wooden villages built out over the water along Weld Quay, in the heart of George Town. Each one was settled by families from a particular Chinese clan, and people still live in them today. The community grew slowly between the 1880s and the 1960s. It began when land was reclaimed along the old shoreline in 1882, which made it possible to build landing jetties for boats and cargo. Seven jetties remain: Ong, Lim, Chew, Tan, Lee, Mixed Clan and Yeoh.

They photograph well because of the repeating lines. Plank walkways run out to sea, stilt houses sit close together on either side, and the George Town skyline rises behind them. Chew Jetty is the most visited of the seven. The recommended viewpoint is the seaward end of Chew Jetty, reached on foot along the boardwalk. From there you look back along the boardwalk and the row of houses towards the city. Tan Jetty and Lee Jetty are good alternatives if you want a different walkway: Tan has a long view out over the water with a red shack at the end, and Lee has colourful houses seen from its entrance.

These are homes, not a stage set. Keep to the main walkway, don't point your phone into open doors or windows, and ask before photographing anyone. Some side branches are private. Part of the fun is the shrines and the small details of daily life, so take your time and keep your shots respectful.
text.geographic_location: The Clan Jetties lie along the coastal road of Weld Quay (Pengkalan Weld) on the waterfront of central George Town, just by the sea edge of the city's heritage core. Chew Jetty is one of the seven, and the subject sits close to it.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops nearby; head to Weld Quay on the George Town waterfront. Ask for Chew Jetty, which is the best known of the seven. Once you reach Chew Jetty, take the walkway out to the seaward end and turn round to face the city. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the boardwalk and the houses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the walkway to run away from you in a long line. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as roof edges, shrines and the skyline in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Chew Jetty (seaward end, facing back toward George Town). The row of stilt houses and the boardwalk running out over the water, with the George Town skyline behind them. Turn to face back towards George Town.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the boardwalk centred, so the planks lead the eye to the skyline. Hold the phone steady and level so the house fronts stay straight. For a different view, try the long walkway on Tan Jetty or the colourful houses seen from the entrance of Lee Jetty. Keep people's doors and windows out of frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the far houses to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the houses don't turn to mush. In dim light, hold still and let night mode finish.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive about 30 minutes before sunset for the warm light. Early morning, before about 9am, also works well, for possible mist and fewer people.

text.access_note: The jetties are living residential communities that visitors walk through on foot, and opening times and access to individual jetties vary, so check locally before you go.

name: Fort Cornwallis
label: Fort Cornwallis
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanade' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jejak Warisan Tembok Laut Esplanade' (way/1201903262): middle (37 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5827552: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Cornwallis' (280 m across).
notes: Star-shaped British fort on the waterfront.

text.description: Fort Cornwallis is the largest standing fort in Malaysia, and it makes a handsome, easy subject for a phone. Low star-shaped brick walls sit right beside the sea, with a slim steel lighthouse at one corner, so one frame can hold sea, walls, gate and sky. The British East India Company built it, and it was finished in 1810 on the site of a simple wooden stockade that Captain Francis Light put up in 1786. It was meant for defence, but in practice it served mainly as an administrative base. The lighthouse dates from 1882, stands 21 m tall and is made of open steel framework. Inside are old cannons, including Seri Rambai, which was cast in 1603 and has travelled a long way since. The former moat was filled in during 1921. Restoration work in 2026 has dug it out again, so the walls now rise from water and greenery once more. For the best outside view, stand on the Esplanade on the waterfront side and face the main entrance gate. The sea gives you a calm foreground and the walls fill the middle of the frame. Keep the horizon level using gridlines, and leave a little space around the gate so the picture feels open. If you go inside, the star-shaped walls and the lighthouse make good close-ups. Part of the fort was closed for restoration, so check current access.
text.geographic_location: Fort Cornwallis stands on the seafront in the old centre of George Town, next to the Esplanade park.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby rail stations or tram stops listed. Head for the Esplanade on the George Town waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and walls with the sea in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sea and sky, and to 2x-3x (or more, depending on your phone) for the gate and the lighthouse.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Esplanade (waterfront side, facing the fort's main entrance gate). The fort's entrance gate and walls in the foreground-to-middle distance, with the sea in front of the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the sea in the lower part of the frame and the gate roughly central, with gridlines on to keep the horizon straight. For a second view, go to the fort's main entrance gate and frame the steel lighthouse at the north-eastern corner. Inside the fort, you can shoot the star-shaped brick walls rising from the restored moat, with the greenery and the lit moat in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and sea keep their colour. Try a Live Photo to catch moving water or passers-by. At dusk, night mode helps if the walls and moat are lit, but hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives golden light on the sea. Morning is easier for the fort walls when you shoot from the Esplanade side.

text.access_note: The Esplanade viewpoint is a free public park, but entry to the fort itself is ticketed and parts were closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Esplanade is a public park beside the fort on the George Town seafront.

name: Little India
label: Little India
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sri Mahamariamman Temple' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sri Maha Mariammam Temple' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6650411: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Lively Indian quarter with shops and garlands.

text.description:
Little India is the Indian quarter in the middle of George Town, and it is one of the most colourful corners of the city to photograph. Shopfronts spill out onto the street with silk and cotton sarees, garlands, spices and jewellery, and there are plenty of restaurants and music shops between them. The oldest Hindu temple in Penang, Sri Mahamariamman Temple, stands here, and its gate is the picture most visitors come for. Many of the Indian fashion shops are mainly on Market Street, so the textile displays make good close-up subjects.

The district is compact and busy, so the best pictures are usually of the street as a whole: signs, awnings, hanging fabrics and people going about their day. Walk to the temple gate and face it to capture its bright colours with the street scene around it. Then walk the nearby lanes, such as Lebuh Pasar for a view down the shopfronts and Lebuh Queen for the textile, flower and food stalls. Street names vary between maps and signs, so check them on the map.

Crowds are heaviest around festivals such as Thaipusam and Deepavali, so allow extra time and patience then. Photography is generally fine in the outer areas of the temple, but please ask before shooting inside.
text.geographic_location: Little India sits in the downtown core of George Town, on Penang island, around the Sri Mahamariamman Temple.
text.directions_text: It is about 75 m south of the district's marked centre, roughly a minute's walk, with the district lying to the north. From there, walk to the Sri Mahamariamman Temple gate, and you can then wander the nearby streets on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the temple gate and general street scenes. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole gate in, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as carvings, garlands and fabric displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outer areas and entrance archway, facing the temple gate). The temple's colourful gate and entrance, with the Little India street scene around it, framed as the district's signature image.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate centred and the vertical lines straight, holding the phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Include a little of the street and shopfronts to show the setting. For a different view, try Lebuh Pasar for a line of colourful shopfronts and signs, or Lebuh Queen for busy stalls selling textiles, flowers and food.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright colours do not wash out. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post. In a busy street, a Live Photo can catch a good moment with people passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk, 6-7pm, when the lamps are lit and the archway and entrance glow. For a quieter scene, one guide suggests arriving before 6am, when devotees gather. Expect crowds around Thaipusam and Deepavali.

text.access_note: The streets are open to the public, but the temple is a place of worship: photography is generally allowed in the outer areas, so ask before shooting inside, and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Visitors to a Hindu temple are usually expected to dress modestly, and may be asked to take off their shoes.
Asking people for permission before photographing them up close is polite and sensible.
The street is narrow enough that the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may be needed to fit the whole gate in.

name: Hin Bus Depot
label: Hin Bus Depot
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hin Bus Depot' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q125131778: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Former bus depot turned art space with murals.

text.description:
Hin Bus Depot is a former bus garage in George Town that now works as an arts and community space, with a gallery, event spaces and small creative businesses. For a phone photographer it is easy to enjoy: an open-air lawn, walls covered in murals, and old brick buildings that give the colourful artwork a plain, textured backdrop. The art deco entrance frame at the gate is a good first picture, and an up-cycled car parked there (Sally Carrera) adds a bit of fun in the foreground.

The depot was built in 1947 along what was then Brick Kiln Road, now Jalan Gurdwara, by Hin Company Ltd. to house its Blue Buses. It closed in 1999, and the buses stopped running in the early 2000s. Later it was refurbished to host the first art exhibition by Penang-based artist Ernest Zacharevic, and the murals here are by him and others. Murals can be restored or repainted, so what you see may differ a little from older pictures.

On Sundays a weekend market, Hin Market, runs here, with around 70 stalls. It brings the lawn to life and makes lively pictures, though it also means more people in your frame. Walk around the lawn and mural garden first, then step back to the entrance for a wider view. Take a few portraits against the exposed brick, as the surfaces are plain.
text.geographic_location: Hin Bus Depot is in George Town, Penang, on Jalan Gurdwara (formerly Brick Kiln Road), in a former bus garage now used as an arts compound.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of George Town and head for Jalan Gurdwara. Use a map app and navigate to Hin Bus Depot, Jalan Gurdwara. Check the address on the day before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the lawn and murals. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the entrance frame or to fit a whole mural wall in from close range.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look across the open-air lawn and the mural walls, with market stalls and greenery framing the old brick buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the mural walls straight and level. Use the brick buildings and greenery as a frame at the edges. For portraits, place your subject in front of plain brick or one mural, a step or two away from the wall. As an alternative, shoot the entrance frame of the old art deco depot from the gate, with the Sally Carrera car in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mural to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich. Portrait mode works well for people against the brick, as long as you keep a little space behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunday is the liveliest, when the weekly market is running and the mural garden is full of life. For fewer people in your pictures, pick another day, but check what is open first.

text.access_note: Hin Bus Depot is an arts compound with events and a weekend market, so check current opening hours locally before you go; hours can vary and photography signs may apply.

name: Komtar
label: Komtar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Penang' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Penang nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/993213417: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'KOMTAR Tower' (71 m across).
notes: Cylindrical skyscraper, the modern city landmark.

text.description:
Komtar is George Town's best-known skyscraper, and from street level it works as a straightforward tall-building shot. The Tun Abdul Razak Complex is a group of five buildings, and Komtar Tower is the tallest. When it was finished in 1985 it stood at 231.7 metres, the tallest skyscraper in Southeast Asia. Renovations in 2015 raised it to 248.7 metres. The complex opened on 2 December 1976 and was designed by Lim Chong Keat as a "city within a city". It sits on a 27-acre superblock and is still a major bus terminal and the seat of Penang's state government.

The tower photographs well because it is so much taller than the blocks around it. Its plain, modernist shape stands out against older low-rise streets, which makes a good contrast between the 1970s plan and the city it replaced. Jalan Penang gives the most direct ground-level view, with the tower rising over the street and the surrounding blocks.

The tower is too tall to fit in a normal frame from close up, so use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and tilt the phone as little as you can. Include a bit of street at the bottom for scale. Traffic and pedestrians come and go, so take a few shots and pick the one with the clearest foreground. If the main street is too busy, Ria Road offers a quieter angle across the low-rise buildings.
text.geographic_location: Komtar stands in the central business district of George Town, on a large superblock beside the Jalan Penang (Penang Road) side. Prangin Mall and 1st Avenue, which grew out of the complex's later phases, are close by.
text.directions_text: Head for the central business district of George Town and walk to the stretch of Jalan Penang in front of Komtar, on the Penang Road side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole tower from base to top from the pavement. Use the default lens (1x) if you can step further back and want less stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for a close-up of the top section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Penang (stretch in front of the tower, on the Penang Road side). Komtar's full height rising over the street and the surrounding city blocks, seen from ground level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and switch on gridlines. Line the tower up with a vertical grid line, and keep the phone as level as you can so the sides don't lean inward too much. Leave a strip of street at the bottom for scale. Ria Road is a quieter alternative, with the tower seen across low-rise buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail. Take a few shots in a row so you have one with a clear foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright, clear day. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the concrete and glass.

text.access_note: The street is a public road with traffic, so take care when framing; for the tower's own attractions or any ticketed areas, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
From the stand-here point, looking east, the tower is lit from behind the photographer in the afternoon.
Jalan Penang is a public road with traffic and pedestrians.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inward.

name: Khoo Kongsi
label: Khoo Kongsi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Khoo Kongsi courtyard' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6832811985: the OpenStreetMap point 'Leong San Tong Khoo Kongsi'.
notes: Ornate Chinese clan house and temple complex.

text.description:
Khoo Kongsi is the grandest clan house in Malaysia, known for its richly carved and ornamented architecture. The complex belongs to the Khoo clan and is the largest Hokkien clanhouse in the country. The temple hall, an association building, a traditional theatre and the clan's old rowhouses are all gathered around a granite-paved square in the oldest part of the city.

The story behind the building is part of its appeal. The clan first built a clanhouse here in 1851. It burnt down in 1901, and the story goes that lightning struck it because it looked too much like an emperor's palace. A smaller version was built from 1902 and finished in 1906, and it is still full of intricate carvings and richly decorated beams. Chinese operas are still staged at the theatre during the seventh lunar month.

For a phone, the best spot is the courtyard, which a heritage walking guide calls the top photo spot in the complex. From there you can take in the whole front of the main hall with its ornate roofline against the sky, then move in on the carvings and gilded beams. The entrance is also a good place to point your phone upwards at the roof ridge. Go early if you can, as mornings are usually calmer, and take a few steps back between shots so the whole facade fits in before you look for detail.
text.geographic_location: Khoo Kongsi stands on Cannon Square in the heart of the oldest part of George Town, within the UNESCO World Heritage area. It is surrounded by narrow lanes and pre-war houses.
text.directions_text: Head for Cannon Square (Lebuh Cannon) in the old heart of George Town, which is where the clan house sits. The old streets are best reached on foot once you are in the heritage area. The temple stands on the square itself and the entrance leads into the courtyard. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard to fit the full front of the main hall and its roof into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the facade. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carvings, gilded beams and roof ridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the full front facade with its ornate roof against the sky, and you can move in on the carvings and gilded beams. The entrance is a second spot where you can look up at the roof ridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the hall up with a horizontal line so the facade does not lean. Leave a little sky above the roof so its outline stays clear. Then zoom in for close-ups of the carvings. For a wider view of the tiered roofline and the ceramic roof figures, Cannon Square outside is a good alternative, as you can stand further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or roof to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the detail in the roof is not washed out. If the carvings look dark, tap on them instead and lift the slider a little.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Between 9 and 10am, when one walking guide says the sun lights the front of the hall. Arriving before 10am also means fewer people in your shots.

text.access_note: The courtyard and interior are inside a clan house that has an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go for opening times and ticket details.

name: Kapitan Keling Mosque
label: Kapitan Keling Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Lebuh Buckingham and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/384337966: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kapitan Keling Mosque' (148 m across).
notes: Indo-Saracenic mosque with a golden dome.

text.description:
Kapitan Keling Mosque is the first permanent Muslim institution in its area of George Town, dating from the early 1800s, and it sits in the middle of the Chulia neighbourhood, part of the city's World Heritage area. It was built in the 19th century by Indian Muslim traders. The land goes back to 1801, when the British Lieutenant Governor, Sir George Leith, appointed Cauder Mohudeen as head of the local South Indian Muslim community and granted him a plot. The building you see today owes its look to a 1930 renovation, which enlarged the mosque rather than rebuilding it and doubled the height of the central prayer hall.

It photographs well because the domes and tall minaret rise above the shophouses along the street, so one frame shows both the mosque and the town around it. Decoration is geometric rather than figurative, which gives the facade clean repeating patterns that look sharp on a phone screen. The mosque is to the north-west from there. Take your wide shot first, then walk closer for details. Please keep your photography outside or in the courtyard and be discreet around people at prayer.
text.geographic_location: In the Chulia neighbourhood of George Town, on the corner of Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (formerly Pitt Street) and Lebuh Buckingham, inside the World Heritage area.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk or navigate from central George Town to the corner of Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling and Lebuh Buckingham. From there the mosque is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade, domes and minaret into one frame from across the street. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the minaret and the domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Buckingham and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (pavement on the opposite side of the street from the mosque's main facade). The white front of the mosque with its domes and tall minaret rising above the street-level shophouses.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the minaret on a vertical line so it does not lean. Leave a little shophouse roofline in the frame to show the street scale. For a different angle, try a side-on view from the Lebuh Chulia approach, which can be quieter; check the angle on the map first. Inside the courtyard, the domes and minarets can be framed by the open space, with the building as the backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the minaret or facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Hold your phone upright and avoid tilting it upwards, to limit leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, just before sunset, when the light on the facade is warm.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship: the worship hall is closed to non-Muslims, modest dress is expected, and photography should stay outside or in the courtyard, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sun Yat-sen Museum Penang
label: Sun Yat-sen Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Armenian' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7619276522: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sun Yat Sen Museum Penang'.
notes: Heritage shophouse where Sun Yat-sen planned revolution.

text.description: The Sun Yat-sen Museum Penang sits in a narrow shophouse on Lebuh Armenian (Armenian Street), in George Town's heritage core. It is worth photographing for its story rather than for grand architecture. The house was built around 1880 as a townhouse and runs back about 40 metres from the street. In 1910 Sun Yat-sen brought his family to Penang and used the house for meetings. That year he chaired an emergency meeting here and raised funds for an uprising in Guangzhou. The first issue of the Chinese newspaper Kwong Wah Yit Poh was also published from this address in December 1910. The house was renovated in 2010-11, with changes to its façade and roof. It is also where the Sun Yat Sen Heritage Trail begins. For a phone photo, the street-level view of the front is the main shot: the narrow shophouse front framed by the street. Take it from the pavement directly in front of No. 120, and look at the façade when you arrive, as the colours and finish may look different from how you expect. Soft early-morning or late-afternoon light suits it best. Inside is a paid museum, so keep your pictures of the exterior unless you have checked the rules for visitors.
text.geographic_location: On Lebuh Armenian (Armenian Street) in the heritage core of George Town, at No. 120, among the old shophouses of the street.
text.directions_text: Navigate on your phone to 120 Armenian Street (Lebuh Armenian) in George Town's old centre. The museum is at that number, and the phone icon on the map is on the pavement right in front of it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straightforward frontal view of the shophouse. If the street is too tight to fit the whole front in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the door and upper front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the museum's narrow shophouse front is right in front of you, framed by the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the front up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Hold the phone upright to show the full height of the narrow house, then take a second shot sideways to include more of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the front keeps its colour and detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sunlight is soft and warm.

text.access_note: The street and pavement are public, but the museum itself is a paid, ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for opening times, tickets and any photo rules inside.

name: Goddess of Mercy Temple
label: Goddess of Mercy
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Armenian' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Lebuh Armenian and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/268531305: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Goddess of Mercy Temple' (97 m across).
notes: Oldest Chinese temple in George Town.

text.description:
The Goddess of Mercy Temple, also known as Kong Hock Keong, is a Buddhist temple in George Town dedicated to Guan Yin. It was built in 1800 and is described as the oldest Chinese temple in Penang. It began as a place to honour Mazu, a sea goddess for seafarers, and by 1824 it had become a Guan Yin temple. It was last renovated between 2012 and 2017.

It photographs well because of its Chinese temple architecture. Sweeping roofs, dragon figures along the ridges, dragon-entwined pillars and large painted doors all sit behind a wide forecourt that faces Pitt Street. Red lanterns and drifting incense add colour and atmosphere.

The viewing corner for the frontage is at the eastern end of Lebuh Armenian, where it meets Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling. It is a free spot on the Armenian Street walking route, and the surrounding heritage streetscape frames the temple well. If you want something different, the walled courtyard at the back is quieter and shows the roofs and ornament in a calmer setting. Close-ups of incense, altars and offerings can be taken in the forecourt and around the compound.

This is a working temple, so be respectful. Ask before photographing worshippers, keep any photography inside discreet, and do not use flash. Incense smoke can be heavy outside, so wipe your lens if your photos look hazy.
text.geographic_location: In the heritage centre of George Town, with its front courtyard facing Pitt Street. The viewing corner is at the eastern end of Lebuh Armenian, where it meets Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling.
text.directions_text: From there, walk north-east towards the temple to reach the frontage view. The viewing corner is at the eastern end of Lebuh Armenian, at the corner with Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling. If you are already walking the Armenian Street route, you can follow Lebuh Armenian to its eastern end and use that corner for the view. Do not confuse this temple with Kuan Yin See on Burmah Road, which is a different site. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage, then use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the forecourt and roof will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ridges, dragon details and lanterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Armenian and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (eastern end of Lebuh Armenian, at the corner with Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling). The temple's street-facing front with its forecourt, roof and red lanterns, framed by the heritage streetscape. Walk north-east towards the temple to reach the street-facing front with its forecourt, roof and red lanterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof ridge up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Keep the lanterns near the top of the frame and some of the street at the edges to show the setting. For an alternative, the quieter walled courtyard at the back shows the roofs and ornament with fewer people. Do not point your phone at worshippers without asking first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red of the lanterns or the temple front to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop bright sky washing out the roof. Switch off the flash. Keep Live Photos on if you want the movement of incense smoke.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day. Early in the day is often calmer for a clear view of the frontage.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress and behave respectfully, ask before photographing people, and check the official site before you go for any access rules.

name: St. George's Church
label: St. George's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Farquhar' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lebuh Farquhar nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124319049: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St George's Church' (56 m across).

text.description:
St George's Church is a white Anglican church in the middle of George Town, finished in 1818 and consecrated in 1819. It is described as the oldest purpose-built Anglican church in Southeast Asia, and in 2007 it was named one of Malaysia's 50 National Treasures. That history shows in the building. A portico of Doric columns leads to a gabled roof, which replaced the original flat roof in 1864, and an eight-sided steeple sits on top. The style mixes Neo-Classical, Georgian and English Palladian. In the grounds, a small domed memorial pavilion from 1886 remembers Captain Francis Light.

The church photographs well because the front is clean, symmetrical and pale against greenery and the street. The best phone view is from across the road, where you can fit the whole front and portico in one frame, with the heritage shopfronts and the street around it. If you want something quieter, try the side and corner angle further along Lebuh Farquhar, where the building's lines run into the street. The lawn view, with the domed memorial and trees in front of the steeple, is another option, but keep to the edges and respect the grounds. This is a working church, so keep quiet and out of the way during services.
text.geographic_location: St George's Church stands in the historic centre of George Town, Penang, on Lebuh Farquhar. The old Court House, where early services were held, was opposite the present church.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops near this spot, so head for central George Town by taxi or hired scooter and ask for St George's Church on Lebuh Farquhar. Once you are at the church, cross to the opposite side of the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road to take in the whole front and portico. If traffic or parked vehicles force you close to the building, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or more to pick out the steeple, but stay level so the columns don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar (across the road from the church). The whole church front and portico seen from the opposite side of the street, showing the building against the street and surrounding heritage shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the portico columns with the vertical lines so the front looks straight. Leave a little street and shopfront in the frame to show the church in its surroundings. For a quieter alternative, walk a short way along Lebuh Farquhar to the corner for the side angle, where the building's lines run into the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the walls keep their detail instead of turning pale. Wait for a gap in the traffic and people before pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Avoid Sunday mornings, when services are held, or shoot only from the street and keep out of the way.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship; photographing from the street is free, but opening hours and rules for going inside vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Traffic or parked vehicles may limit how far back you can stand on Lebuh Farquhar.
Taxis or hired scooters are available for getting to central George Town.

name: Sri Mahamariamman Temple
label: Sri Mahamariamman
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Queen' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lebuh Queen nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/591291871: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Maha Mariammam Temple' (41 m across).
notes: Colourful Hindu temple with a sculpted gopuram.

text.description:
Sri Mahamariamman Temple is the oldest Hindu temple in Penang, and it sits right on a busy George Town street. Its main draw for photographers is the entrance: a brightly painted gopuram (the tower over the gateway) and a facade crowded with sculpted gods and goddesses. The temple is usually dated to 1833, though accounts vary on the exact year. It is still an active place of worship. Processions for festivals such as Navarathiri and Chitraparuvam have set out from it, which gives you a sense of how much it matters to the local community.

The colours and detail are what make it work on a phone. By backing across Lebuh Queen you can fit the whole gateway into the frame with the street around it. Then you can step closer or zoom in to pick out individual figures. Keep your pictures to the outside of the building. Photography inside is generally not allowed, and worshippers should not be disturbed, especially during prayers. If you want a calmer picture, walk round to the back of the temple on Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling. The rear facade is a quieter angle with fewer people in the way. Allow a few minutes to look at the facade properly before you start shooting. The sculpture is dense, and a slow look will help you choose which part to photograph.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of George Town, on Lebuh Queen (Queen Street), with its rear side facing Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling.
text.directions_text: Start from central George Town and head to Lebuh Queen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the whole gateway, backing across the street if you can. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if passing people or parked vehicles force you to stand close. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sculpted figures above the entrance arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lebuh Queen (across from the front entrance, looking back toward the gopuram). The brightly painted gopuram and the sculpted facade above the entrance arch, framed by the street. Backing across the street gives a wider view of the whole gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the gopuram with the middle vertical line, so the tower looks straight. Keep your phone level and tilt it up only slightly to avoid leaning verticals. Include a little of the street at the bottom to give a sense of place. For a quieter second angle, try the rear facade from Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Take a few frames, as people walk through the scene constantly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the colours. The temple may close for a break around midday, so check the opening hours before you go.

text.access_note: This is an active Hindu place of worship: shoes and hats must be removed to go in, photography inside is generally not allowed, and opening times and rules can change, so check the opening hours before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines and a level phone help keep a tall tower looking straight.
Passing people and vehicles on the street may get in the way of the shot.

name: Armenian Street
label: Armenian Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Armenian' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lebuh Armenian nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18378689: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Armenian Street' (317 m across).
notes: Famous for street art and heritage shophouses.

text.description:
Armenian Street is a narrow, shophouse-lined street inside George Town's UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it has become popular for street art. It is home to the famous 'Children on a Bicycle' mural by Ernest Zacharevic, painted on a shophouse wall with a real bicycle attached. The pavement is a comfortable place to shoot straight on, or you can step in and pose beside the bicycle.

The street has plenty of history too. It began as a Malay lane, and by 1808 it had taken its name from the Armenian traders who lived along it. Chinese families later took over much of the street and built clan houses nearby. In 1910 Sun Yat-sen chaired a conference in a townhouse here, which is now a museum. All of this shows in the facades, which give your mural pictures a good backdrop.

Its exact wall should be checked on the map once you arrive. Take one close, straight-on shot of the wall, then step back for a wider one that includes the neighbouring shopfronts. For a different view, a long look down the street shows the shophouses receding into the distance. The 'Kids on Swing' mural at Lorong Love, a side lane off the street, is a second option. Murals can fade, so check what is currently on the wall.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of George Town's UNESCO World Heritage Site, on Lebuh Armenian, close to the junction with Lebuh Cannon. Clan houses, small museums and antique and souvenir shops line the street.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Lebuh Armenian on foot or with a map app. Confirm the exact wall on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on shot of the bicycle mural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long view down the street, where you want to fit in the facades on both sides. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for tighter crops of the painted faces, which also leaves out passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lebuh Armenian (at the Zacharevic 'Little Children on a Bicycle' mural, near the junction with Lebuh Cannon). The painted children on a real bicycle fixed to a shophouse wall, framed by the heritage facades along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the wall square to the frame so the shophouse lines stay straight. Take one tight shot of the mural, then a wider one with the street around it. If you want to pose with the bicycle, ask a friend to shoot from the pavement. For an alternative, try the long perspective down Lebuh Armenian, or the 'Kids on Swing' mural at Lorong Love, where the side lane opens behind the corner wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the painted wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or bright walls wash out the colours. Portrait mode works well for a person posing next to the bicycle. Check that the edges of the frame are clear of strangers before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide recommends early morning, around 7–9am, before the tour groups arrive. Other guides favour late afternoon or sunset. Crowds are heaviest from late morning to mid-afternoon and at weekends, and Chinese New Year is very busy, though the lanterns make it colourful.

text.access_note: The street itself is an open public street, but the museums along it may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Lebuh Aceh Mosque
label: Lebuh Aceh Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Acheh' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Lebuh Acheh and Lebuh Cannon (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/264411523: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Acheen Street Mosque' (72 m across).

text.description:
Lebuh Aceh Mosque, also known as the Acheen Street Mosque, is a 19th-century mosque in George Town. It was built in 1808 on land given by Tengku Syed Hussain Al-Aidid, an Acehnese aristocrat who had opened a Muslim settlement in the area in 1792. That settlement grew into a centre of Islamic study, visited by traders from across the Malay archipelago, Arabia and India. In the 19th century the area was sometimes called the Second Jeddah, because pilgrims gathered here before sailing to Mecca. The houses around the mosque are part of that original settlement, and the founder's family cemetery lies next to it.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the compact scene. The three-tiered minaret rises above the street near the corner with Cannon Street, with older shophouses lining the street below it. Standing near the corner gives you a street-level frame of rooftops, minaret and sky that works well in both portrait and landscape. If you have time, a second view is the mosque's façade, with the courtyard and palm-shaded entrance behind it. A third is down the lane, with the mosque at the far end and shophouse fronts close on either side.

This is a working place of worship, so keep a respectful distance from anyone praying, dress modestly near the entrance and avoid prayer times if you want to go closer. Take a few frames from near the corner first, then decide whether to walk in.
text.geographic_location: In the old Muslim quarter of George Town, on Lebuh Acheh (Acheen Street), near the corner with Cannon Street. The mosque is surrounded by the historic shophouses and houses of the area.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of George Town, in the old heritage area, and head for Lebuh Acheh. The distance is short, and the last stretch is on foot from the heritage area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the street scene, with the shophouses leading to the minaret. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the street. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to isolate the minaret against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Acheh and Lebuh Cannon (corner where the mosque's street meets Cannon Street). The minaret rising above the corner, framed by the historic shophouses on the street. The position is approximate, so adjust a few steps as needed. The mosque itself lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and keep the minaret near one third of the frame, with shophouse rooflines on one side. Switch on gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. For a second picture, walk a little way down the lane and frame the mosque at the end, with shophouse fronts in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the minaret to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white walls do not burn out. Try a Live Photo if people are walking through the lane, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets. Try to avoid prayer times if you want to go closer to the entrance.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship. You can see it from the street, but dress modestly near the entrance, respect worshippers at prayer times and ask at the entrance before going inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The street is fairly narrow, so the ultra-wide lens helps fit the shophouses and minaret into one frame.
Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people in the lane.
Tapping the minaret and lowering the exposure will help keep detail in a bright sky and white walls.
The last stretch to the mosque is on foot from the heritage area.

name: Jubilee Clock Tower
label: Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lebuh Light' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Lebuh Light and Lebuh Pantai (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6301836: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: White Victorian clock tower near Fort Cornwallis.

text.description: The Jubilee Clock Tower, also called the Queen Victoria Memorial Clock Tower, stands where Light Street meets Beach Street, next to the moat of Fort Cornwallis. It was built to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee and was paid for by the Chinese business leader Cheah Chen Eok. Building began in 1900, and the tower was opened on 23 July 1902. It was designed by the municipal engineer Robert Peirce in the Indo-Saracenic style, and it rises about 30 metres (97 feet) to the top of its copper-roofed cupola. Each of the 60 feet up to the clock is said to stand for one year of the Queen's reign. It photographs well because the tower is framed against the colonial street corner, with the clock face, the belfry and the cupola all easy to read from the street. The tower leans slightly after bomb damage in the Second World War, so don't be surprised if the lines look a little off. It was restored between 2019 and 2020. Because it stands in the middle of a busy roundabout, take your photos from the pavement at the corner and cross carefully. You can only see it from outside, as the interior is not open to visitors. If the junction is busy, try the quieter King Edward Place, on the museum side, for a calmer view of the tower.
text.geographic_location: At the junction of Light Street and Beach Street in George Town, beside Fort Cornwallis and its moat. The tower stands in the middle of the roundabout there.
text.directions_text: Head for the junction of Light Street and Beach Street in George Town, as there is no station or tram stop nearby. Take care with the traffic: the roundabout has wide avenues and no nearby pedestrian crossing. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and the street corner around it into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Light and Lebuh Pantai (junction of Light Street and Beach Street, the corner by the tower). The full Moorish-style tower framed against the colonial street corner, with the clock face visible. If the junction is busy, King Edward Place on the museum side is a quieter alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, as it is tall and the lines can look tilted if you aim the phone upwards. Keep the phone level and step back a little rather than tilting it. Include a bit of the street corner and the nearby buildings to give a sense of place. For a second shot, zoom in on the clock face and the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock face to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the tower keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case a vehicle drives through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best for seeing the clock face and the architectural detail. Early in the day is likely to be quieter for traffic, but check how the light falls on the day.

text.access_note: The tower is an open public landmark in a busy roundabout that you can view from the street; the interior is not open to visitors, so check the official site before you go if you want to confirm access.
